newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-European bourses down, ignore Wall St boom.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-European bourses down, ignore Wall St boom.

text.p: European stocks were mixed on Thursday with investors distracted by interest rate worries and ignoring Wall Street which hit another record overnight, the 10th this month.
On currency markets, the dollar was firm against the mark and climbed half a yen after Japanese authorities shut down a troubled bank, the first time they have done so in five decades.

Gloomy European markets, for the most part, drew no comfort from the bull run in in New York. The Dow Jones average closed at 6,430.02 points on Wednesday, beating the record set the previous day and chalking up its 41st new high this year.

Domestic issues depressed most bourses on this side of the Atlantic, decoupling them from the New York rally, which was driven by gains in General Motors shares. Europe frequently takes a lead from Wall Street.

In London, stocks were down at mid-morning but had recouped some initial losses suffered as the market became more preoccupied by sterling's strength, interest rates and the possibility of unwelcome news in next week's budget.
Dealers said investors feared that finance minister Kenneth Clarke might indulge in pre-election tax cuts in next Tuesday's budget despite rising inflationary pressures.
"It would blow his credibility and the Bank of England would howl so I can't see it myself. But the uncertainty is enough to keep everyone flat in this market," another trader said.

Investors were still unsettled by British figures issued on Wednesday showing stronger-than-expected October retail sales, which re-ignited interest rate anxieties. The mood was not helped when figures showed Britain's second quarter trade surplus was the best for 10 years.

"The failure of the UK to respond to Wall Street just raises tensions and we are being held back by the budget. Worse, the data yesterday and today have encouraged people to anticipate a quarter-point rate rise before Christmas," one dealer said.

In Frankfurt, stocks were down slightly at mid-morning in listless trading which dealers said lacked direction. Volumes in early computer trade were thin, with interest low even in newly-floated Deutsche Telekom shares.
French shares clawed back initial losses but volumes were thin. Dealers said the market trend was positive but Friday's monthly settlement could weigh on prices.
"No one has really any desire to buy ahead of the settlement," said one trader.

The dollar was stronger against the yen but underlying support for the Japanese currency came from Japan's robust September diffusion index of leading indicators which showed the economy was continuing to recover gradually.
Currency traders were keeping a close eye on Japan's banking sector after the closure of Hanwa Bank Ltd, suffocating under 190 billion yen ($1.7 billion) in problem loans.
The dollar also strengthened against the mark after the Bundesbank's policy-making council on Thursday decided to leave German interest rates unchanged.
While a rate change had not been expected, traders said markets had been marking time ahead of the Buba announcement.
CURRENCIES AT 1220 GMT
The dollar was quoted at 111.70 yen and 1.5007 marks, compared with 111.17 yen and 1.4960 marks in late European trade on Wednesday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1220 GMT
LONDON - The Financial Times-Stock Exchange index of 100 leading British shares was down 1.8 points at 3,961.0.
PARIS - The CAC-40 share index was up 9.37 points at 2,242.76.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index was down 2.27 points at 2,772.23.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was fixed at $378.50 an ounce, compared to Wednesday's close of $379.15. Silver was down two cents at $4.94.
